title: Two survivors rescued in Nepal 10 days after catastrophic floods - Vatican News
description: Two survivors rescued in Nepal 10 days after catastrophic floods  Vatican News
publisher.title: Vatican News
full_article:
By Linda Bordoni

Read also 29/08/2026 In wake of devastating floods, Pope sends aid to Nepal Through the Dicastery for the Service of Charity, Pope Leo XIV has sent financial support to Caritas Nepal as relief operations continue and the death toll in the affected regions ...



According to authorities, the man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower plant in Nepal, which was struck by flash floods that washed away valleys and buried entire villages on 26 August.

The rescued woman was found alive inside a damaged house in Nuwakot town and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.

At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

A joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts has been trying to reach surviving workers in the 12 hydropower stations across Nepal where some 900 people are missing, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels.s

Meanwhile, geophysicists say that satellite images from just days before the collapse of rock and ice that triggered the catastrophe suggest that a section of the glacier and the rocks it sat on top of were accelerating in the weeks before the actual collapse.

However, the precise sequence of events remains unclear, and experts say such events are difficult to predict using existing monitoring techniques.

What they do agree upon is that with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50 percent faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks.

title: Portland’s Nepali community grieve and organize aid after devastating flooding - Oregon Public Broadcasting - OPB
description: Portland’s Nepali community grieve and organize aid after devastating flooding  Oregon Public Broadcasting - OPB

full_article:
In this undated photo provided by Mercy Corps, aid workers in the Nuwakot district provide support to victims in the week following Nepal’s devastating flash floods. Courtesy of Kreepa KC / Mercy Corps

Catastrophic flash flooding along the Tibet-Nepal border on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,300 people and thousands more are still missing, according to local authorities.

THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR: Become a Sponsor

International aid groups are on the ground distributing food and shelter to people whose homes and entire communities were swept away or severely damaged.

“People who somehow saved their lives, they have nothing left,” said Suraj Sidel, Mercy Corps’ Nepal Country Director, who is based in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu. The Portland-based nonprofit is currently passing out basic necessities like hygiene kits, cookware and mosquito nets to over 700 affected families in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.

Daily news in your inbox OPB's "First Look" is your guide to Northwest news and culture, delivered to your inbox every weekday and Saturday morning. Email Please leave this field blank Sign up

Sidel said the damage is bigger than the 2015 earthquake in Nepal that killed over 8,000 people. The death count from the flood is still rising as emergency rescue teams struggle to reach remote villages and people blocked by debris and water.

This photo provided by Mercy Corps shows a building submerged underwater on Sept. 2, 2026, in Bidur, Nepal, after a glacial collapse triggered flash floods on Aug. 26, 2026. The floods have wiped out entire villages and made it difficult for emergency response teams to perform rescue operations and recover dead people. Courtesy of Kreepa KC / Mercy Corps

Right now, people are extremely traumatized, said Pratap Maharjan, Mercy Corps’ emergency response team leader on the ground in Nuwakot.

“The most heartbreaking thing [is] to see the pain in the eyes of people who have not slept for days with fear of another flood coming in,” he said.

A tight-knit Nepali community in Portland mobilizes to grieve and support one another

Seven thousand miles away at a Buddhist temple in Portland, a small but tight-knit community of Nepali Americans have been grappling with the loss.

As one of the only temples outside of Asia that practices the Newar Buddhism that originated in the Kathmandu Valley, the Nritya Mandala Mahavihara has been a special place of worship for Nepalis living abroad.

“This temple has been doing a lot of work to protect the Nepalese kind of Buddhism in America,” said Rabin Shakya, a Nepali journalist based in Portland. “All the life rituals are carried on at this temple.”

In this photo provided by Ganga Sharma, people gathered on Aug. 30, 2026, for a vigil at the Nirtya Mandala Mahavihara Buddhist temple in Portland, honoring flood victims in Nepal. Courtesy of Ganga Sharma

Last Sunday, people gathered at the Nritya Mandala Mahavihara to grieve the loss of life in Nepal.

Ganga Sharma attended the somber, candlelit event with her sisters. As an executive member of the Nepali Association of Oregon, Sharma has been fundraising for disaster relief to help rebuild the flooded districts.

THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR: Become a Sponsor

“This is massively huge, it’s global,” Sharma said of the flood’s impact. Because of the flood, the Nepali Association of Oregon and other organizations have canceled their annual Teej festivities that celebrate women and girls.

Right now, the focus is on recovery and survival. Several of Sharma’s friends have lost family members or know people who lost their homes. “It’s all washed out. They’ve got no place to go,” she said.

In 2015, Sharma and the Nepali Association of Oregon raised just over $60,000 to help rebuild Nepal in the aftermath of the 7.8 magnitude earthquake.

Related: Nepal warns of possible fresh flooding as communities grapple with devastation

This time they are collecting donations through Zelle and she hopes they can match their previous fundraising efforts through community support. The Nepali Association of Oregon will be hosting another vigil for flood victims on Sept. 20 at Pioneer Courthouse Square in downtown Portland.

“Every penny will be welcomed for donations towards the disaster relief fund,” said Sharma.

Even during this heavy moment for her community, Sharma doesn’t want this disaster to overshadow what her culture and country have to offer people.

“Please don’t be afraid to visit Nepal … It’s a beautiful country, Nepal, it survives on tourism,” she said. “The hospitality of Nepalese people is very kind and generous.”

Related: A melting glacier contributed to the deadly Nepal floods. We can expect more like this

Oregonians rally to support flood victims

Mimgma Sherpa grew up in Nepal, spending summers as a mountain guide in his youth. He moved to Portland on the suggestion of his American clients who lived here. Now a chef, he sells Himalayan eats out of Sherpa Kitchen at the ZED in Southeast Portland.

Sherpa has collaborated with Zoiglhaus Brewing Company to make 80 gallons of their unique Himalayan pilsner. The pilsner will be sold at the Zoiglhaus brewery, and at the Norte Taproom in Wilsonville and the Hollywood Q in Northeast Portland throughout this weekend.

“We’ve been doing it as a seasonal beer for us, but since this tragic event has happened it just made sense to make it again to try to help people,” said Taylor Melvin, the operations manager for the brewery. Proceeds from the sales of the Himalayan pilsner will go towards Khangri Experience Foundation, a nonprofit based in Washington working to address the emergency needs of children who are flooding victims in Nepal.

Cook Marco Martinez prepares a dal bhat, a Nepali lentil curry, at Sherpa Kitchen in Portland, Ore., on Sept. 2, 2026. The restaurant is collaborating with a local brewery to raise disaster relief funds for victims of Nepal's massive floods. Jireh Deng / OPB

Sherpa said he’s additionally donating 50% of his food sales this weekend to the Khangri Experience Foundation, which was founded by Sherpas living in the Pacific Northwest.

Support efforts are still gaining momentum, but Portland journalist Rabin Shakya said he’s already been overwhelmed by the kindness of his neighbors.

Steve March, a former Oregon state legislator, happens to buy a newspaper every day at the local 7-Eleven that Shakya and his wife work at. This past week he also dropped off a note with a check for the flood victims.

“It’s not money, it’s just his gesture that’s important,” Shakya said. “This is a time to be in solidarity, in unity with the flood affected people.”

title: Ground Report: Bridges Washed Away, Zipline Keeps Nepal's Devighat Connected - ndtv.com
description: Ground Report: Bridges Washed Away, Zipline Keeps Nepal's Devighat Connected  ndtv.com
publisher.title: ndtv.com
full_article:
After the Nepal floods, Devighat's beauty has become unsettling. The Trishuli River, swollen and moving with a fierce, muddy current, cuts through the picturesque landscape. Around 20 metres from the water body, the ground is littered with the broken remnants of the lives of those who lived here just ten days ago.

A slipper of an adult, half-buried in the silt; a much smaller slipper, belonging to a child; a damaged suitcase, lying half-open; a guitar, left behind among the mud, rocks and debris -- they are all ordinary objects in ordinary times. They now serve as haunting monuments of lives upended by the flash floods.

Beyond this strip closest to the river, the devastation stretches further inland. Within roughly 50 to 60 metres of the banks, homes have been ripped apart, uprooted or reduced to their foundations.

Further up, on the slight rise, buildings that stood away from the immediate riverbank have also been badly damaged. It is as if the river came through and erased the settlement in layers.

The bridge that once connected the two sides of Devighat is gone. All that remains is the staircase that once led up to it.

A flight of steps, standing alone, leading nowhere. Right beside it are the foundations of homes that once stood along the riverbank. Iron rods jut out from broken concrete. Rocks and fragments of walls are all that remain. It looks as if the homes have been uprooted from the earth itself.

Also read: Reporter's Diary: 10 Days In Nepal And Stories That Never Reached The Camera

And the river keeps moving.

The Trishuli has now become a symbol of both a physical and emotional divide. Bridges have been washed away, and their essential duties are now being performed by a 250-metre zipline suspended above the river.

And even the zipline tells the story of what happened here.

On one side of the river, its ropes are fastened to an iron rod jutting out of the ground, one of the few remnants of a home destroyed by the flood. On the other side, the ropes are secured to a banyan tree. One end is anchored to what remains of a destroyed house; the other to a tree that survived. It is an unlikely bridge between two banks, and between what Devighat was and what it has become.

People now use it to move across the river, carrying food, essentials and belongings.

Keeping that lifeline running are local volunteers. They work in three-hour shifts, rotating through the day. They have been here since morning, helping people cross and moving supplies between the two sides.

When we asked one of the volunteers whether he was afraid that someone could fall from the zipline, his response was striking.

The flash flood had come and gone, he said. The force of the water did not scare them, so what was this compared to that? he added.

The river has already shown them what fear looks like. And so they keep working. For now, the zipline is the only link between the two sides.

But a bridge is being built. The Nepal Army is working to reconnect the two banks, with the new bridge expected to take another three to four days to complete. Until then, this thin cable remains the lifeline for residents who have no other way across.

Also read: 'World Hasn't Seen This Before': Expert On "Extraordinary" Nepal Rescue Op

However, rebuilding here is not easy. The rains continue to hamper construction, relief and rescue operations.

When we arrived at Devighat, it was sunny. When we left, it was pouring nonstop.

Across the devastated areas, excavators and diggers are at work, pulling out and clearing the enormous quantities of soil deposited by the flood. But even walking through some parts of Devighat is difficult.

The ground is still waterlogged and unstable, covered in deep, loose silt. Residents trying to cross it find their feet sinking into the earth. Some struggle to pull themselves free.

The landscape has been physically altered, and it is difficult to know what is safe to stand on, let alone where it is safe to rebuild.

For Dipak Sunar, the consequences of the flood are waiting at home. Dipak is a banker. He was not at home when the flood struck. His brother was. So were his parents, his other brothers and their families. When the mudslide came, they ran towards higher ground.

They survived. But they could not return home.

Today, the family is living at a relief centre in a school.

Dipak walks us towards the two-storey family home where he was born. The house stands about 150 metres from the banks of the Trishuli. The ground floor has been badly damaged. Around the house, the earth is covered in soft, unstable silt. The soil is so fragile that the house can no longer be considered safe to live in.

Before showing us his own home, Dipak points towards another concrete building closer to the river. The flood moved it roughly 50 to 70 metres from where it once stood, leaving it partly buried in the earth.

It is difficult to comprehend the force required to move a concrete building that distance.

Then Dipak takes us to his own house. This is the place where he was born. The place where his parents lived. The place his brothers and their families called home. But for now, none of them can return.

"The mudslide was so devastating. We can't return for five or six months," Dipak says.

Just ten metres away is another family home-Sitaram Remalchi's. And the contrast between the two could not be more stark.

When we met Sitaram, he was carrying a bag filled with kitchen utensils from his motorcycle to the place where his home once stood. His father built this house.

Sitaram had lived here for 40 years. Now, almost nothing is left.

The entire house has been swept away, except for a part of the kitchen at the back.

On a surviving concrete wall, the impression of the bed that once stood against it can still be seen. A trace of a room. A trace of a life.

Sitaram remembers how quickly it happened. "Everything was fine at first, then within 25 minutes, everything was destroyed," he says.

They were warned about the flood only moments before it hit.

Sitaram and his family ran towards higher ground to save their lives. They survived. But the place they had called home for four decades was gone. His family has rented accommodation for now. When asked how long it would take to rebuild, Sitaram says he does not know. But he is not sure he wants to rebuild here at all.

He says the place is unsafe now. He would rather move somewhere safer.

He does not want to put the lives of future generations at risk. Ten metres separate Sitaram's home from Dipak Sunar's. Yet the flood has left them with two very different realities. For one family, the home is still there, but the earth beneath it has become too unstable to live on. For the other, there is barely a home left to return to.

What remains of both families' lives now has to be carried, moved and pieced together elsewhere. And that is where the zipline takes on a different meaning.

It is no longer simply a way to cross a river. It is how people are continuing to live.

For Masina Nepali, the flood was a story of a decision made in seconds. She was near the river with her daughter when the flash flood struck. There was no time to think.

She grabbed her daughter by the arm and ran uphill. That instinct saved their lives. Her home was not spared. Today, Masina walks through the devastated riverbank carrying essentials on her head, secured with a cloth strap.

The Trishuli flows behind her, swollen and fast. Her home is across the river. She uses the zipline every day to carry essentials across and take them back to her house.

Her daughter is sick and in hospital. Even as she deals with that, Masina is trying to salvage what she can from a home that has been devastated. The zipline has become part of her daily life.

As it has for Raju Rimal. His family is on the other side of the Trishuli. His parents, his brothers and their families were all living there when the flood struck.

When we meet him, he stands beside the zipline and looks across the river. He whistles. He calls out to his family. Then he waves.

For a moment, it is an ordinary exchange between a family separated by distance. Except that the distance now exists because the bridges are gone.

Raju remembers the day the flood came. He says he warned his family and villagers to run. "Run, the flood has hit us, rush," he shouted. He says around 200 people were saved that day.

But his own home and village were severely damaged. Houses, clothes and food were swept away in the floodwaters.

Food is now scarce. Moving from one place to another has become a daily struggle. Raju and his family also had a furniture shop. That too is gone. Today, when he wants to reach his parents, his wife and his children, he has to use the zipline.

For Raju, this has already become routine. A journey that once would have been unthinkable is now simply part of the day.

That may be the most striking thing about Devighat. The extraordinary has become ordinary. A 250-metre zipline over a swollen river is now a daily means of transport. A school has become a relief centre. A family home has become unsafe to live in. A four-decade-old house has been reduced to a kitchen. Excavators work through the mud as the Nepal Army races to rebuild the bridge. And the rain keeps coming.

Along the riverbank, the remnants of ordinary lives remain scattered in the mud. A slipper. A child's slipper. A suitcase. A guitar.

The Trishuli still flows past them, swollen and powerful. The bridge is gone. The homes are broken. The community has been physically divided. But people have found another way across.

For now, that thin line suspended above the Trishuli is more than a zipline. It is the thread holding Devighat together.

title: Relatives hold cremations without bodies for Nepal’s missing flood victims - Al Jazeera
description: Relatives hold cremations without bodies for Nepal’s missing flood victims  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nepal – Nine days after his father, Dinesh, went missing, Sujan Achhami, 23, carries a body to the bank of the Bagmati River next to the famous Pashupatinath Temple in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. He lays the body on the Brahmanal – a stone on which corpses are placed for rituals. The priest reads mantras, directing Sujan to wash the body and offer a traditional clay lamp and flowers.

Except it’s not a real body.

Catastrophic flash floods swept through northern and central Nepal on August 26, killing more than 1,200 people and leaving almost 5,000 others missing. With hopes of finding them alive – or even dead – fading, grieving relatives are being forced to say goodbye without bodies. So, many are instead performing symbolic last rites using effigies made of sacred kusha grass.

“We searched for them everywhere,” says Khim Bahadur Gharti Magar, whose uncle Tham Bahadur Pun, 71, a former British Army soldier, and aunt Chausara Pun, 64, were on a pilgrimage in northern Nepal when the flood hit. “We couldn’t find them.”

He has also performed these symbolic last rites for his missing relatives, right here on the bank of the Bagmati.

“There were 17 buses in the group they were with. During our search, we found four other people [dead bodies] who were part of the pilgrimage group. That’s why we decided to cremate,” Magar says.

Sher Bahadur Pun, the deceased man’s son-in-law and a senior health official with the Nepal government, says the family has given DNA samples to police in the hope their identities might be traced later.

Advertisement

For Dinesh Achhami’s family, the search for the 41-year-old has been equally devastating. A driver from Barabishe municipality in northern Nepal, Achhami was in Rasuwa – the district hit worst by the floods – at the time the surging waters barrelled down from Tibet. “We looked everywhere because we had no clear idea where he was hit,” says his uncle Raju Achhami.

Maniram Tharu narrowly survived the flood while working at the Upper Trishuli 1 hydropower project. His 30-year-old brother Dipendra – also a hydropower worker who was employed in a different, downstream project – and sister-in-law Phool Maya Tamang, in her 40s, have been missing since the flood.

“I cannot find their names on the list of those reported safe,” he says. “We don’t know where to go, what to do. We are worried. They have small children who are safe because they are living with other family members.”

Sujan Achhami (front) helps to carry a symbolic effigy of his father, Dinesh, who died in deadly flash floods and a mudslide, for a cremation ceremony because his body has not been recovered, at Pashupatinath Temple in Kathmandu, Nepal, on September 3, 2026 [Adnan Abidi/Reuters]

Temporary burials

The scale of the disaster has overwhelmed the authorities. Nepal Police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle says storing recovered bodies remains a major challenge.

“The proper way would have been to preserve bodies until identification is established but we are not in that condition,” he says. “Many bodies are already in very bad shape, decomposed, some even in pieces, and cannot be preserved for extended periods.”

So authorities are temporarily burying unidentified bodies – with the aim of exhuming them and handing them to relatives once their identities are established.

Out of 1,344 bodies recovered so far, a total of 1,030 bodies have been buried in this way. Just 96 bodies have been handed over, after being identified by families, authorities say.

According to Kafle, the bodies have been properly numbered and have been buried at various sites in Chitwan, Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Kathmandu, Pokhara and other regions of Nepal.

But, he said, police have collected DNA samples from all bodies found so far before their burial, “to enable identification and matching with families later”.

Many in Nepal have been outraged by the government ‘s decision to carry out mass temporary burials of the deceased, describing it as going against Hindu religious traditions.

At the bank of the Bagmati next to Pashupatinath Temple, a veteran priest tells Al Jazeera that the past two days have been among the busiest he has witnessed since the 2015 earthquake, in which nearly 9,000 people died. Then, he said, most families “at least had bodies” to cremate.

As Nepal deals with its latest humanitarian crisis, the priest is this time helping carry out the symbolic cremations. He says they’re legitimate, according to Hindu scriptures. But that families are having to perform symbolic rituals is still a tragedy, he says.

“It’s a terrible scene here,” he says.

full_article:
Rescuers in Nepal have pulled a Chinese hydropower worker and a Nepali woman alive from the wreckage left by catastrophic flooding, as search teams continue combing the region for thousands of people still missing.

Lu Haitao was freed on Saturday from 225 metres inside a flooded tunnel at a hydropower plant in Rasuwa district, in the mountains north of the capital, Kathmandu.

Recommended Stories list of 2 items list 1 of 2 Nepal rescues two workers from hydropower tunnel nine days after floods

Nepal rescues two workers from hydropower tunnel nine days after floods list 2 of 2 Moment two workers are pulled alive from Nepal tunnel end of list

Separately, 64-year-old Chandika Kumari Shrestha was dug out of her collapsed home in the neighbouring district of Nuwakot.

Both had been trapped since a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas on August 26, unleashing a torrent of water, rock and ice that swept through the valley.

Coming within hours of each other, the rescues are the third and fourth in days, and have renewed hope that more of those still unaccounted for in the region’s flooded tunnels could be found alive.

Lu was brought out by a joint team of Nepali soldiers and South Korean disaster specialists, and appeared stable though mildly hypothermic as he was flown by helicopter to a hospital in Kathmandu.

Speaking afterwards to Chinese state television, he described calling out to rescue crews whenever he glimpsed their torchlight in the tunnel, only to go unheard each time, until a beam finally swept over him. “I couldn’t believe it,” he said.

Al Jazeera’s Tony Cheng, reporting from Rasuwa district, said rain on Saturday had slowed the search there, though rescue teams were continuing to push ahead.

Shrestha, found covered in mud inside her flooded house, was given water by rescuers before being airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment, officials said.

Advertisement

Her rescue followed that of two Nepali tunnel workers pulled alive a day earlier from a nearby hydropower site, the first survivors recovered from any of the region’s damaged plants.

More than 1,300 dead, 5,000 still missing

The disaster has now killed at least 1,331 people in Nepal and left about 5,000 people missing, including 589 foreign nationals, according to the country’s national disaster authority.

Meanwhile, officials in Tibet, the autonomous region of China across the border, have recorded 31 deaths and 531 people missing.

About 900 workers remain unaccounted for at hydropower construction sites alone, with roughly 500 of them believed to still be trapped inside tunnels across a dozen projects wrecked by the floodwaters.

The glacier collapse that triggered the disaster sent debris crashing into towns and villages built along river valleys that Nepal has relied on for hydroelectric power, destroying roads, homes and schools in an area popular with foreign trekkers and pilgrims.

Search teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have since joined the operation, along with a 15-member Australian drone unit sent this week, after Nepal asked for outside help in a rescue effort that had relied mainly on its own forces.

One of the survivors freed from the Trishuli 3A tunnel this week told rescuers that other workers were still alive further inside, the Nepali army said, and officials say further searches are now focused on that site.

Nepal’s information and communications minister, Bikram Timilsina, said authorities remained hopeful that more people would be found alive. “We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” he said.

full_article:
Two more survivors from Nepal’s catastrophic flash floods were rescued on Saturday, offering a sliver of hope for a region reeling from the destruction wrought by a wave of water, ice and mud that washed away entire riverside communities 10 days ago.

A Chinese national, Lu Haitao, was pulled from the hydropower tunnels where hundreds of other workers remain missing while the other, 60-year-old Chandika Shrestha, was found downriver, on the upper floor of a four-story building in the devastated community of Betrawati.

So much time has passed since the floods that Shrestha’s family had started ceremonial last rites and begun preparing for her funeral, believing she had died, a local official said.

Thousands of families remain in this limbo across Nepal and China, not knowing if their loved ones are alive or dead. At least 1,362 people are known to have died in the disaster, authorities say.

About 900 of those missing are hydropower workers, who were working at facilities dotted along the Trishuli River when a huge chunk of ice sheared off a melting glacier, triggering a landslide and floods which buried entire communities in minutes.

Lu said he had been desperately trying to attract rescue workers’ attention for days, crying for help whenever he saw their lights.

“Whenever I saw the lights, I shouted, ‘Hey!’ Really loudly, really loudly,’ he told Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. “Maybe they didn’t hear me.

“When they came to rescue me today, even when their (lights) were shining right in front of me, I couldn’t believe it.”

Nepal Army

Two other workers were rescued on Friday from a different hydropower plant after rescuers had worked around the clock in treacherous conditions in the hope of finding survivors.

But away from these miraculous rescues, the death toll continues to rise – two bodies were recovered from the same site where Lu was found – and other families are still enduring an agonizing wait for news of missing relatives.

Krishna Poudel added an image of his younger brother Ishwor, a 26-year-old hydropower worker, to a board with scores of other such posters for those missing eight days ago, but he still doesn’t know his brother’s fate.

Some who escaped from the tunnels told Poudel that his brother is still inside, he told Reuters. “They said they could hear the voices of about 200-300 people shouting from inside,” he said.

Related article Nepal army soldiers work during a search and rescue operation outside a tunnel near the Hydropower Project sites in Rasuwa district, Nepal, in this handout obtained on September 2. NEPAL ARMY/Handout/Reuters ‘Don’t panic’: How two men were rescued from a flood-stricken Nepali power plant 5 min read

Rescue teams, helped by specialist crews from other countries including India and China, are concentrating their efforts on these hydropower stations. But authorities are also working to rescue those who found themselves cut off by the floods and to rebuild temporary bridges across the river, the Nepali Army said Saturday.

More than 7,500 homes across Nepal and around 55 kilometers (34 miles) of road were damaged in the floods, the Nepali Foreign Ministry said Saturday, leaving thousands in need of humanitarian assistance but with access to the area severely restricted.

Around 35,000 people are believed to need safe temporary accommodation, while 43,000 are feared to be at immediate risk of food insecurity, according to a United Nations report.

With such urgent humanitarian assistance required, dozens of US Congress members have written to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, calling on him and his department to “do much more.” That, they suggested, should include providing daily updates to family members of missing Americans, share aerial imagery with first responders, and provide additional reconstruction support.

A State Department spokesperson told CNN “we do not comment on Congressional correspondence.” They pointed to the $3.6 million already committed to the relief effort, and said an additional $3 million in assistance “will be provided through our global assistance award with World Food Programme.”

full_article:
After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts

Thousands remain missing and aid is hampered by treacherous conditions in communities almost wiped out of existence

By Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel / The Guardian, Nepal

Add TT as Preferred Source



Searching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house.

On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats.

As deadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet.

A member of the Nepal Army on Thursday walks out of a damaged building near the entrance of a tunnel at Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station following the deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Rasuwa, Nepal. Photo: Reuters

Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of meters high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him.

“When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said.

displayDFP('ad-IR1', 'm');

He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China.

Nepal Armed Police Force on Tuesday carries a dead body to transfer by helicopter from Dhunche, in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photo: Reuters

Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself.

“Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears.

The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbor’s house once stood.

A Nepal Army helicopter on Wednesday carries dead bodies from the flood affected area in Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Photo: AFP

“Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”

UNIMAGINABLE TRAGEDY

The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8:37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8:50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed.

A Nepal Armed Police Force helicopter carrying relief supplies on Tuesday lands for flood affected people in Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Photo: AFP

This once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 meters from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was.

Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them.

As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath.

Rescue team members on Thursday work to enter the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station as they search for survivors and retrieve bodies, following deadly flash floods and a mudslides in Rasuwa, Nepal. Photo: Reuters

“I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.”

A few meters away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone.

“My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.”

VILLAGES SWEPT AWAY

Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far.

A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters.

The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing.

Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing.

“There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.”

He stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.”

With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north.

At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakantha school, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes.

Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students.

“Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.”

However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.”

For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead. Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.”

It was, added his wife, “a miracle.”

Ghale told NewsCenter 5 he lost friends and close family members when flooding broke out in his home country in late August.

Others in his village ran for their lives as water overtook vehicles and homes. Ghale and his wife woke up to a phone call from his cousins as the disaster unfolded.

"He said, 'Then we ran uphill,' back of his house is uphill so they ran as much as they could and his and his wife survived, his older sister was behind his wife; she couldn't make it, so these are the stories that I've heard from him," said Ghale. "It's almost like a nightmare, and I still- I'm still... hard to believe."

He said his family's village is a small one.

Ghale is raising money in response to the disaster and is planning to go there next week. The funds will be used for food, water, medical supplies, and temporary housing for the victims, according to Ghale's GoFundMe.

In a week from now, leaders and representatives of BRICS nations will descend upon New Delhi to attend the 18th summit of the international group which India is hosting as part of its 2026 presidency.

The summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital.

Preparations are entering their final stage ahead of the meet and Delhi is set to be a fortress with a heavy security blanket.

On Saturday, a motorcade rehearsal had been scheduled with the traffic authorities in Delhi issuing an advisory for diversions and regulated movement on key routes.

The Indian Express has reported that drones would be deployed to track the movement of traffic and spot chokepoints during the summit.

Meanwhile, media reports earlier this week said that hotel prices in the capital were soaring around the dates of the summit.

Indian news outlets said that luxury hotels in the city were either fully sold out or were giving rooms at a significantly higher tariff.

For one luxury hotel in central Delhi, a room that costs 23,000 Indian Rupees (€210, $243 approx) a night this weekend was listed at 280,000 Indian Rupees (€2,550, $2,963 approx) per night from September 10 to 13, with the rates going back to normal from September 14th, a search on a travel app showed.

India's fourth round of BRICS chairship

BRICS is an 11-member bloc which brings together major emerging markets and developing countries of the world.

India said the upcoming meet will also be joined by partner countries and outreach invitees.

The group's presidency rotates annually among the member states.

India, which is also a founding member of BRICS, has previously held the presidency thrice — in 2012, 2016 and 2021.

India's BRICS chairship is guided by the theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," according to a statement by the foreign ministry in New Delhi.

description: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.

The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.

Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.

Rescue of Nepal hydropower workers ‘triumph for humans and humanity’, tunnelling expert says Read more

Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment.



Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.

At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.
